editorialPolicy.storyFidelity: The twelve sessions preserve the complete original 36-chapter arc, causal sequence, major choices, consequences, reunions, and ending.
editorialPolicy.foundation: Concrete, speakable sentences with one main action and mostly 6–11 words per line.
editorialPolicy.core: Connected sentences with cause, contrast, and reaction, mostly 10–18 words per line.
editorialPolicy.studio: Literary but performable sentences that preserve narrator wit, suspense, and moral tension.
editorialPolicy.safety: Historic peril and slapstick retain their narrative consequence without added graphic detail.
editorialPolicy.narration: Generate one continuous master per session and level; Watch and Mimic must seek within the same performance.
editorialPolicy.classTime: The story text remains concise; sixty minutes comes from deliberate replay, recording, comparison, retrieval, and sentence reconstruction—not padding the narration.

narration.direction: Keep the school fight fast but not triumphant, emphasize the reciprocal rescue between Pinocchio and Alidoro, and end with earned hope rather than instant perfection.
narration.productionRule: Generate one continuous master per session and level; Watch and Mimic seek within that exact same master.

livingStorybook.artBrief: A coastal stage links the book fight, wounded classmate, officers, Alidoro's sea chase, Green Fisherman's net and kitchen, Fairy's slow door, study desk, and promised celebration.

lines.text: At the beach, there was no Shark.
The classmates had lied and started a fight.
They threw schoolbooks like heavy stones.
One book struck a boy named Eugene.
The other boys fled before the officers arrived.
The officers blamed Pinocchio and arrested him.
A police dog named Alidoro chased him.
Alidoro fell into the sea, so Pinocchio saved him.
Later, a Green Fisherman caught Pinocchio in a net.
The Fisherman planned to fry him for dinner.
Alidoro returned and carried Pinocchio to safety.
Pinocchio hurried back to the Fairy's house.
The slow Snail made him wait all night.
His impatient kick trapped one foot in the door.
For many months, Pinocchio studied and worked faithfully.
The Fairy promised he would become a boy tomorrow.

lines.text: At the beach, Pinocchio discovered that the Shark story was a lie.
His classmates mocked him, and their argument became a violent book fight.
A heavy schoolbook struck Eugene, leaving him injured on the sand.
The guilty boys ran away before the officers could question them.
Because Pinocchio remained beside Eugene, the officers blamed and arrested him.
He escaped, but the powerful police dog Alidoro chased him into the sea.
When Alidoro began drowning, Pinocchio turned back and saved his pursuer.
The dog promised to repay the unexpected act of kindness.
Soon a Green Fisherman pulled Pinocchio from the water in a net.
Mistaking him for a rare fish, the cook prepared to fry him.
Alidoro arrived at the last moment and carried Pinocchio away.
The rescued puppet finally returned to the Blue Fairy's house.
A painfully slow Snail left him waiting outside through the night.
Pinocchio kicked the door, trapped his foot, and regretted his impatience.
During the following months, he studied, worked, and rebuilt the Fairy's trust.
At last, she promised that he would wake as a real boy the next day.

lines.text: The beach contained no Shark at all; the story had been invented to pull Pinocchio away from school.
Mockery became an argument, and the classmates converted their schoolbooks from tools of learning into weapons.
One heavy volume struck Eugene, who collapsed while the sea carried the evidence back toward shore.
The boys responsible fled, leaving Pinocchio beside the injured student when the officers arrived.
His decision to remain looked like guilt, and the authorities arrested the one person attempting to help.
Pinocchio escaped, but Alidoro, a powerful police dog, pursued him through the waves.
When the exhausted dog began to drown, Pinocchio abandoned escape long enough to save his pursuer.
Alidoro remembered the mercy and promised that kindness would not remain unpaid.
A Green Fisherman soon hauled Pinocchio from the sea inside a net crowded with fish.
Convinced that the wooden creature was an exotic catch, he coated the prisoner and prepared the frying pan.
Alidoro burst into the kitchen, recognized his rescuer, and carried Pinocchio beyond the cook's reach.
The puppet reached the Fairy's home expecting comfort, but the Snail required him to wait through the night.
Impatience returned in one furious kick, leaving Pinocchio's foot trapped in the door and his breakfast made of imitation food.
The humiliation taught what repeated promises had not: change needed patience when nobody offered immediate applause.
For months Pinocchio studied, worked, and allowed dependable behavior to rebuild the Fairy's trust.
Satisfied by the evidence, she promised that the following morning would finally begin his life as a real boy.
